nameStory: The 'thin-walled maze polypore' gets its name from the intricate maze-like pattern on its underside, where the pores stretch and twist into labyrinthine shapes as the fungus ages. The 'thin-walled' part refers to the delicate walls between these maze passages. It's also called the 'blushing bracket' because it turns pink or red when you touch or bruise it, like it's embarrassed to be discovered!
description: This is a bracket fungus that grows like a shelf or semicircle from the sides of dead or dying hardwood trees. The tough, leathery fruiting body can reach up to 8 inches across and has distinctive concentric zones of brown colors on top, like tree rings. The underside starts whitish but turns gray-brown with age, and here's the cool part – it bruises pink or red when touched. Instead of regular round pores, mature specimens develop an intricate maze-like pattern underneath.

idTips.label: Bruising
idTips.description: Touch the white or grayish underside and watch it turn pink or red within minutes – this color-changing reaction is the best way to confirm your identification

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Semicircular and tough as leather, with concentric bands of brown, tan, and gray colors radiating from where it attaches to the tree

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Start as tiny round holes but stretch into long, winding maze-like slits and channels as the fungus matures – run your finger along them to feel the raised walls

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels like thick, dry leather or cardboard – tough enough that you can't easily tear it with your hands

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always growing from dead or dying hardwood trees, especially willows, never on conifers or on the ground

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Fresh specimens have a mild, pleasant mushroomy smell, while older ones may smell slightly sour or musty

habitat: Look for this bracket fungus on dead or dying hardwood trees throughout New England's forests, with willows being a favorite host. You'll find it from lowland wetlands up to mid-elevation forests, anywhere deciduous trees are present. It's particularly common along streams and in mixed forests where hardwoods like birch, maple, and oak provide plenty of potential hosts.

seasonality.spring: Existing fruiting bodies from previous seasons are still present and identifiable, often showing the clearest bruising reactions as they're refreshed by spring moisture.
seasonality.summer: New growth begins on fresh wounds in trees, appearing as small white brackets that gradually develop their characteristic zoned patterns.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for fresh, actively growing specimens with the most pronounced color changes and clearest maze patterns developing on the undersides.
seasonality.winter: Persistent year-round, old fruiting bodies remain attached to trees and are still identifiable, though colors may be faded and bruising reactions slower.

funFact: This fungus is like a tree surgeon gone rogue – it specifically targets wounded hardwood trees, acting as nature's way of cleaning up after storms, logging damage, or other injuries by breaking down the damaged wood with its white rot.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other bracket fungi like Turkey Tail or False Turkey Tail, but the instant pink bruising reaction makes identification foolproof – no other common New England bracket changes color so dramatically when touched.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'Daedaleopsis' refers to Daedalus from Greek mythology, the craftsman who built the famous labyrinth – a perfect reference to this fungus's maze-like pore structure that becomes more intricate with age.
compareHints: While its close relative Daedaleopsis septentrionalis (Northern Daedaleopsis) also bruises when touched, it tends to be more northern in distribution and has slightly different pore patterns. The thin-walled maze polypore is much more common in New England and has more pronounced concentric zoning on the upper surface.
